Consider the statements about lengths.
Statement 1: 41/10 is read 'forty-one tenths' and is the same as 4 1/10.
Statement 2: 4/10 is longer than 4 1/10 because its numerator is the same but it has no whole part to subtract.
Statement 3: 10 one-tenths make 1 unit, so 130/10 is 13 units.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:

Reason (R): 63 tenths are 60 tenths, which is 6 units, plus 3 tenths.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Match each length in Column I with the same length in Column II.
Column I: 1. 36/10   2. 306/100   3. 63/100   4. 63/10

A screw is 4 8/10 cm long and another is 4 1/10 cm long. (a) Write the length of the first screw in tenths only. (b) By how many one-tenths is it longer than the second screw?
questions.a: (a) 4 8/10 = 40/10 + 8/10 = 48/10, i.e. 48 tenths. (b) The second is 41 tenths, so the first is longer by 48 - 41 = 7 tenths (7/10 cm).
s: Part (b): finds 41 tenths for the other and the gap of 7 tenths

questions.q: A pencil is 5 3/10 5/100 cm long (5 units, 3 tenths and 5 hundredths). (a) Write its length in hundredths only. (b) A second pencil measures 548/100 cm. Which is longer and by how many hundredths?
questions.a: (a) 5 units = 500 hundredths, 3 tenths = 30 hundredths, so 535/100. (b) 548 hundredths is more than 535 hundredths, so the second pencil is longer by 13 hundredths.
s: Part (b): compares 548 with 535 and states the gap of 13 hundredths

questions.q: Explain why 10 one-tenths make 1 unit but it takes 100 one-hundredths to make the same unit.
questions.a: A unit is split into 10 equal parts to get tenths. Each tenth is split again into 10 equal parts to get hundredths, so one unit holds 10 x 10 = 100 hundredths.
s: States that a unit is split into 10 equal parts to make tenths
States that each tenth is split into 10 to make 10 x 10 = 100 hundredths in a unit

questions.q: (a) Read 4/10 and 41/10 aloud in words. (b) Write both as mixed forms where possible and find how many tenths longer 41/10 is than 4/10.
questions.a: (a) four-tenths and forty-one tenths. (b) 4/10 is already less than one unit; 41/10 = 4 1/10. The difference is 41 - 4 = 37 tenths, i.e. 3 7/10 units.
s: Part (b): writes 4 1/10 and finds the difference of 37 tenths

questions.q: Arrange in increasing order: 38/10, 3 5/10, 3/10, 83/10. Say how you compared them.
questions.a: 3/10 < 3 5/10 < 38/10 < 83/10. Write each as a mixed form: 0 3/10, 3 5/10, 3 8/10, 8 3/10; compare the units first, and the tenths where the units tie.

questions.q: Imran says: '43/100 cm is longer than 4 3/10 cm, because 43 is more than 4 and 3.' Is he right? Explain with the units.
questions.a: No. 43/100 is 43 one-hundredths, which is less than 1 unit (it is not even half a unit). 4 3/10 is more than 4 units. So 4 3/10 cm is longer.
s: Gives the verdict that Imran is wrong
Shows 4 3/10 is more than 4 units so it is longer

questions.q: A helper writes a length as '6 12/10' and says this is a mixed form with fewer than 10 tenths. Show that this is impossible and rewrite the length correctly.
questions.a: 12/10 is 12 tenths, which is more than 10 tenths, so it makes 1 whole unit and 2 tenths. A mixed form with fewer than 10 tenths cannot hold 12 tenths. 6 12/10 = 6 + 1 + 2/10 = 7 2/10.
s: Notes 12 tenths is more than 10 tenths (more than 1 unit)
Explains the extra unit must move to the whole part

questions.q: Create a real-life situation in which a length of 53/10 units is measured. Then write that length as a mixed form.
questions.a: Any sensible story, e.g. a tailor measures a strip of lace as 53 one-tenths of a metre. Mixed form: 53/10 = 50/10 + 3/10 = 5 3/10 m.
s: Gives a realistic measuring situation that uses 53/10

questions.q: A school rope-climb rope was knotted from three pieces of lengths 2 7/10 m, 3 6/10 m and 1 9/10 m. (a) Write each piece in tenths only. (b) Add them in tenths. (c) Write the total as a mixed form. (d) A new rope is 80/10 m long. Which rope is longer and by how many tenths?
questions.a: (a) 27/10, 36/10, 19/10. (b) 27+36+19 = 82 tenths. (c) 82/10 = 8 2/10 m. (d) 80/10 = 8 m = 80 tenths; the knotted rope has 82 tenths, so it is longer by 2 tenths.
s: Part (a): converts the three pieces to 27, 36 and 19 tenths
Part (d): compares 82 with 80 tenths and says the knotted rope is longer by 2 tenths

questions.q: A craft teacher cuts strips of length 3/10 m, 3/100 m, 33/100 m and 30/100 m. (a) Write all four strips in hundredths. (b) Arrange them from shortest to longest. (c) Two of the strips are equal. Name them and explain why they are equal.
questions.a: (a) 30/100, 3/100, 33/100, 30/100. (b) 3/100 < 3/10 = 30/100 < 33/100. (c) The 3/10 m strip and the 30/100 m strip are equal: each tenth is 10 hundredths, so 3 tenths = 30 hundredths.
s: Part (a): converts 3/10 to 30/100 and keeps the others in hundredths

questions.q:
Ramesh, a tailor in Jaipur, has three pieces of lace for a lehenga border: 2 7/10 m, 3 5/10 m and 1 8/10 m. The customer's border needs 8 1/10 m. The shop sells extra lace only as a 2/10 m cut (₹60 each) or as one 1 m piece (₹90). The customer may also order a matching dupatta trim that needs 5/10 m more.
(a) Write the 3 5/10 m piece in tenths only.
(b) Find the total of the three pieces in tenths.
(c) By how many tenths is the lace short of 8 1/10 m?
(d) The customer says she will probably order the trim as well. Compare buying 2/10 m cuts with buying the 1 m piece, in length and in cost, and decide.
questions.a: (a) 35/10. (b) 27 + 35 + 18 = 80 tenths = 8 m. (c) 81 - 80 = 1 tenth short. (d) With the trim he needs 81 + 5 = 86 tenths, which is 6 tenths more than he has. That takes three 2/10 m cuts (₹180) but one 1 m piece (10 tenths, ₹90) covers it with 4 tenths to spare. If she orders the trim, buy the 1 m piece; if she orders only the border, a single 2/10 m cut (₹60) is enough.
s: Part (c): finds the shortage of 1 tenth
Part (d): needs 6 tenths with the trim, compares 3 cuts at ₹180 with one piece at ₹90, and states the conditional choice

questions.q:
For sports day at a school in Nagpur, Chhaya prepares medal ribbons. The gold ribbon is 1 3/10 6/100 m, the silver ribbon is 1 2/10 9/100 m and the bronze ribbon is 1 1/10 15/100 m. Every ribbon must be at least 1 3/10 m long to go round a medal neatly.
(a) Write the gold and silver ribbons in hundredths only.
(b) Which is longer, and by how many hundredths?
(c) Write the bronze ribbon with fewer than 10 hundredths in the last place.
(d) Which ribbons can Chhaya use without buying new ribbon? Give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Gold = 130 + 6 = 136/100; silver = 120 + 9 = 129/100. (b) Gold is longer by 7 hundredths. (c) 15 hundredths = 1 tenth + 5 hundredths, so bronze = 1 2/10 5/100 (125/100). (d) Needed length 1 3/10 m = 130/100. Only the gold ribbon (136) is at least 130; silver is 129 and bronze is 125, both short.
s: Part (d): compares each with 130 hundredths and says only gold can be used

s: Part (a): writes 203.04 with 0 as the tenths placeholder
Part (b): reads it and names the hundredths place for the 4

questions.q: Why is a decimal point needed to write 4 units and 2 tenths? What would '42' mean instead?
questions.a: Without a point, 42 would be read as 4 tens and 2 units. The decimal point marks where the whole-number places end and the tenths begin, so 4.2 and 42 are different quantities.
s: States that 42 means 4 tens and 2 units
States that the point separates the whole part from the fractional part so 4.2 differs from 42

questions.q: (a) How many tenths make one ten? (b) How many hundredths make one ten?
questions.a: (a) One ten is 10 units and each unit has 10 tenths, so 100 tenths. (b) Each unit has 100 hundredths, so one ten has 10 x 100 = 1000 hundredths.
s: Part (b): 1000 hundredths with the reason 10 x 100

questions.q: Aditi reads 0.508 as 'zero point five hundred and eight'. Correct her and say what the digits 5, 0 and 8 stand for.
questions.a: It is read 'zero point five zero eight'. The 5 stands for 5 tenths, the 0 for no hundredths and the 8 for 8 thousandths; digits after the point are read one by one.
s: Reads it correctly as zero point five zero eight
Names the places: tenths, hundredths (zero), thousandths

questions.q: Meena says: 'To measure something smaller than a unit we must always split the unit into 10 parts; splitting it into 4 equal parts is not possible.' Is she right? Why do we still prefer 10?
questions.a: No. A unit can be split into 4, 5, 8 or any number of equal parts, and each quarter can be split into 4 again to give 16 parts in a unit. We prefer 10 because each place in our system is 10 times bigger than the one on its right, so tenths and hundredths extend the system naturally.
s: Gives the verdict that Meena is wrong
Says a unit can be split into other numbers of parts, such as 4 (then 16)
Explains that 10 is used because place values change by a factor of 10

questions.q: Show that a single digit in the tenths place can never be worth as much as 1 unit, even for the largest digit 9.
questions.a: The largest digit is 9, and 9 tenths = 0.9. It takes 10 tenths to make 1 unit, so 9 tenths is 1 tenth short of a unit. A digit in the tenths place is therefore always less than 1 unit.
s: Takes the largest digit 9 in the tenths place and gets 0.9
States 10 tenths are needed for 1 unit
Concludes 0.9 is less than 1 so no tenths digit reaches 1 unit

questions.q: Create a real-life situation in which moving the decimal point of 2.5 one place to the right (to 25) would cause a problem. Say how many times the quantity changes.
questions.a: Any realistic story, e.g. a recipe or weighing: 2.5 kg of sugar is mistaken for 25 kg. The value becomes 10 times as large because each digit now sits in a place worth 10 times as much.
s: Gives a realistic situation using 2.5 and 25
States what the wrong reading means in that situation
States the quantity becomes 10 times bigger

questions.q: Write each quantity as a decimal: (a) 3 ones, 4 tenths and 6 hundredths; (b) 2 tens and 8 tenths; (c) 5/100 and 3/10 together; (d) 4 hundreds and 7 hundredths. Then (e) read the decimal in (d) aloud.
questions.a: (a) 3.46. (b) 20.8. (c) 3/10 + 5/100 = 0.35. (d) 400.07, with zeros holding the tens, units and tenths places. (e) four hundred point zero seven.
s: Part (c): 0.35 by adding 3 tenths and 5 hundredths
Part (e): reads four hundred point zero seven

questions.q: Find the decimal form of (a) 15 tens and 15 tenths; (b) 30 ones, 30 tenths and 30 hundredths; (c) 8 tens, 8 ones, 8 tenths and 8 hundredths. (d) Which of the three is the largest, and which is the smallest?
s: Part (b): 33.3 by converting 30 tenths and 30 hundredths
Part (d): picks 151.5 as largest and 33.3 as smallest

questions.q:
In a school science fair in Pune, a group shows five heaps of rice. The first heap weighs 1 g, and each next heap is 10 times as heavy as the one before it. Their display table has a scale that can read only up to 12 kg.
(a) What does the third heap weigh in grams and in kilograms?
(b) What is the combined weight of the five heaps in kilograms, as a decimal?
(c) In your answer to (b), name the place value of the digit in the tenths place.
(d) Can the group put all five heaps on the scale together? If they add a sixth heap by the same rule, will it fit on the scale? Give reasons.
questions.a: (a) 100 g = 0.1 kg. (b) 1 + 10 + 100 + 1000 + 10000 = 11111 g = 11.111 kg. (c) The tenths digit is 1, standing for 1 tenth of a kg (0.1 kg = the 100 g heap). (d) 11.111 kg is less than 12 kg, so all five can be weighed together. The sixth heap is 100000 g = 100 kg, far above 12 kg, so it cannot.
s: Part (a): third heap is 100 g = 0.1 kg
Part (b): adds the five heaps to 11111 g = 11.111 kg
Part (c): names the tenths digit as 1 tenth of a kilogram
Part (d): 11.111 kg < 12 kg so five fit; the sixth heap of 100 kg does not

questions.q:
A school lab in Chennai must choose a new measuring scale for a unit length. Scale P splits each unit into 4 equal parts and each quarter again into 4 equal parts. Scale Q splits each unit into 10 tenths and each tenth again into 10 hundredths. The lab records readings as decimals, and some experiments need differences as small as 0.01 of a unit, but each class has only 30 minutes to read the scale.
(a) How many smallest parts make one unit on scale P and on scale Q?
(b) Which scale can show smaller differences, and how do you know?
(c) A reading on scale Q is 2 units, 3 tenths and 7 hundredths. Write it as a decimal.
(d) Which scale should the lab choose? Give one advantage and one drawback of your choice.
questions.a: (a) P: 4 x 4 = 16 parts; Q: 10 x 10 = 100 parts. (b) Q: its smallest part is 1/100 of a unit, smaller than 1/16, because more parts fit in a unit. (c) 2.37. (d) Scale Q is the better fit: its smallest part, 0.01, matches the smallest difference needed and each place is 10 times smaller, so readings write directly as decimals. The drawback is 100 marks per unit, which are slower to read than 16 on scale P. A student who values speed over fineness could defend P, but then differences of 0.01 cannot be read.
s: Part (a): 16 parts on P and 100 on Q
Part (b): chooses Q because 1/100 is smaller than 1/16
Part (d): weighs the 0.01 requirement against reading time and justifies the choice

(a) Write 0.6 with two digits after the point and with three digits after the point. (b) Is 0.06 equal to either of them? Use place value to say why.
questions.a: (a) 0.60 and 0.600 (6 tenths = 60 hundredths = 600 thousandths). (b) No. 0.06 is 6 hundredths, while 0.60 is 60 hundredths; the 6 sits one place to the right.

questions.q: From the numbers 3.6, 3.06, 0.306, 3.600, 3.60, 3.006 and 03.60: (a) list those equal to 3.6. (b) Of the remaining three, which is the smallest, and why?
questions.a: (a) 3.600, 3.60 and 03.60. (b) 0.306 is the smallest: it has 0 units, while 3.06 and 3.006 each have 3 units.
s: Part (b): picks 0.306 and gives the units-place reason

questions.q: Use place value to explain why 0.2 and 0.20 are the same quantity.
questions.a: 0.2 is 2 tenths. Each tenth is 10 hundredths, so 2 tenths = 20 hundredths, which is written 0.20. The quantity is the same; only the place it is counted in has changed.
s: Converts 2 tenths to 20 hundredths and concludes the quantity is unchanged

questions.q: (a) Write 64 ones, 8 tenths and 70 hundredths as a decimal. (b) Write the same value with exactly three digits after the point.
questions.a: (a) 70 hundredths = 7 tenths, so 64 + 0.8 + 0.7 = 65.5 (the same as 65.50). (b) With three digits after the point it is 65.500.
s: Part (a): regroups 70 hundredths as 7 tenths and gets 65.5

questions.q: State the rule about zeros at the right end of a decimal. Give one example where a zero cannot be dropped.
questions.a: Zeros written after the last digit on the right of the decimal point do not change its value (0.3 = 0.30 = 0.300). A zero that sits between the point and a non-zero digit cannot be dropped, e.g. 0.02 is not 0.2.
s: States that zeros at the extreme right do not change the value
Gives a valid example such as 0.02 versus 0.2

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Writing 0.5 as 0.500 does not change it, but writing it as 0.05 does.' Is he right? Support your answer with place value.
questions.a: Yes. 0.5 is 5 tenths = 500 thousandths, and 0.500 is also 500 thousandths, so the extra zeros at the right end change nothing. 0.05 is 5 hundredths = 50 thousandths, because the zero put right after the point moves the 5 to a smaller place. The statement is true because it separates the two kinds of zero.
s: Gives the verdict that Kabir is right
Shows 0.05 is 50 thousandths because the zero was added just after the point

questions.q: Show that 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005 cannot be made equal by adding zeros on the right of each.
questions.a: Written in thousandths: 0.5 = 500/1000, 0.05 = 50/1000, 0.005 = 5/1000. Adding zeros at the right only changes the number of places used; the three amounts stay 500, 50 and 5 thousandths, which are all different.
s: Writes the three in a common place (500, 50, 5 thousandths)
Notes added right-hand zeros do not change a value

questions.q: Write three different decimals that all equal 4 tenths, and one similar-looking decimal that does not. Say why the last one is different.
questions.a: 0.4, 0.40 and 0.400 are all 4 tenths. 0.04 looks similar but is 4 hundredths, one tenth of 0.4, because the 4 has moved one place to the right.
s: Gives three valid equal forms of 4 tenths
Explains with place value that it is 4 hundredths

questions.q: A grocer in Indore labels five rice packets in kg: 2.50, 2.5, 2.05, 2.500 and 0.25. (a) Which labels show the same weight? (b) How many different weights are there? (c) List the different weights from lightest to heaviest. (d) By how many hundredths of a kg is 2.5 heavier than 2.05?

Sonu says 0.2 can be written 0.20 and 0.200. Zara says adding zeros may change the value. (a) Write 0.2, 0.20, 0.200 and 0.02 in thousandths. (b) Who is right about the first three? (c) By how many thousandths does 0.2 exceed 0.02? (d) State what Zara should have said so that she is also right.
questions.a: (a) 200/1000, 200/1000, 200/1000 and 20/1000. (b) Sonu: all three are 2 tenths. (c) 200 - 20 = 180 thousandths. (d) Zeros added at the right end do not change the value; zeros added just after the point do (0.2 becomes 0.02).

Part (b): says Sonu is right for the first three
Part (d): states the condition: right end only, not after the point

questions.q:

(a) Which of the four recorded weights are equal to 1.25 kg?
(b) Write 1.25 kg with three digits after the point and say how many thousandths of a kg the part after the point has.

Part (d): finds shortfalls 225 and 45 thousandths and chooses 1.025 first

questions.q:
Aarav wants a geometry box from one of four shops in his Delhi market that display prices Shop A ₹24.50, Shop B ₹24.5, Shop C ₹24.05 and Shop D ₹2.45. The boxes are the same make. Shop D's board is a hand-written sign that the owner has not updated for a month.

(c) 24.50 / 2.45 = 10: 10 times smaller, the same digits with the point moved one place. s: Part (c): 10 times smaller, and says the point may be misplaced so he should ask the shop first

For each pair in Column I, choose in Column II the place whose digits first decide which number is greater.

On a number line, point P is at the 7th mark when the gap from 3 to 4 is cut into 10 equal parts, and then at the 4th mark when the gap from 3.7 to 3.8 is cut into 10 equal parts. (a) Write the decimal for P. (b) Is P greater or less than 3.8, and by how many hundredths?
questions.a: (a) P = 3.7 + 4 hundredths = 3.74. (b) P is less than 3.8; 3.80 - 3.74 = 0.06, which is 6 hundredths.

questions.q: A number line from 0 to 2 is divided into 10 equal parts. (a) What does each mark stand for, and what decimal is at the 3rd mark? (b) Which mark shows 1.4?

s: Part (a): each mark is 0.2 and the 3rd mark is 0.6

questions.q: Compare 1.009 and 1.090. Say at which place you can stop comparing and why.
questions.a: 1.090 is greater. Units (1) and tenths (0) are equal, and at the hundredths 1.009 has 0 while 1.090 has 9. We can stop there because nothing in the thousandths can make up a difference of hundredths.
s: Names the hundredths place as the first difference and explains why we can stop

questions.q: Arrange these masses in descending order: 8.304 g, 8.34 g, 8.043 g, 8.4 g, 8.399 g. Name the digit that decided between the first two.
questions.a: 8.4 > 8.399 > 8.34 > 8.304 > 8.043. All have 8 units; the tenths digits are 4, 3, 3, 3, 0, so 8.4 is greatest. Between 8.399 and 8.34 the tenths tie at 3 and the hundredths 9 > 4 decide.

questions.q: The gap between 2.4 and 2.5 on a number line is cut into 10 equal parts. Write the decimal numbers at the 3rd and 8th division points.
questions.a: Each part is one hundredth. The 3rd point is 2.4 + 0.03 = 2.43 and the 8th point is 2.4 + 0.08 = 2.48.

questions.q: Raj says: '6.4999 is greater than 6.5 because it has more digits and a lot of 9s.' Is he right? Explain why the extra 9s cannot rescue it.
questions.a: No. 6.5 = 6.5000. The units are equal; the tenths are 4 and 5, so 6.4999 is less. The digits after the tenths place add less than 1 tenth in all (0.0999 < 0.1), so they cannot reverse the result.
s: Gives the verdict that Raj is wrong

Explains the remaining digits add less than 1 tenth

questions.q: Show that no decimal with only one digit after the point lies strictly between 3.6 and 3.7. Then name a decimal with two digits that does.
questions.a: One-digit decimals are whole numbers of tenths: 3.6, 3.7 differ by exactly 1 tenth, so no whole number of tenths lies strictly between them. Splitting the gap into 10 equal parts gives hundredths such as 3.65, which lies between them.

Gives a two-digit example such as 3.65

questions.q: Write two decimals A and B such that A has more digits after the point than B and A is smaller than B. Then write two decimals C and D where C has more digits and is larger. Explain what decides each pair.
questions.a: For example A = 5.382 and B = 5.4: A has more digits but is smaller since the tenths 3 < 4. And C = 5.41 and D = 5.4: C has more digits and is larger since 5.41 > 5.40. The first place where the digits differ decides, not the number of digits.

questions.q: To locate 7.46 on a number line you magnify the line step by step. (a) Between which two whole numbers do you start? questions.a: (a) 7 and 8. (b) 7.4 and 7.5. (c) The 6th mark (7.4 + 6 hundredths). (d) Less than 7.5 by 4 hundredths (0.04).

questions.q: In a javelin event at a school meet in Bhopal, five throws (in metres) are 31.38, 31.083, 31.8, 30.99 and 31.308. (a) Rank them from longest to shortest. (b) Which throw won, and which was second? (c) By how many hundredths of a metre did the winner beat the second place? (d) Which digits decided the order of the 2nd and 3rd throws?
questions.a: (a) 31.8, 31.38, 31.308, 31.083, 30.99. (b) 31.8 won; 31.38 was second. (c) 31.80 - 31.38 = 0.42, i.e. 42 hundredths. (d) 31.38 and 31.308 tie at 31 units and 3 tenths; the hundredths decide (8 versus 0).
s: Part (d): says the hundredths (8 versus 0) decide

questions.q:
At a school sports day in Mysuru, five girls ran the 100 m race. Their times in seconds were Aisha 14.28, Bhavna 14.082, Chitra 14.8, Dolly 14.208 and Esha 14.265. The district team takes the two fastest runners who ran under 14.25 seconds. One reserve may also be named, and the rules allow a reserve only if her time is within 0.02 seconds above 14.25.
(a) Arrange the girls from the fastest (smallest time) to the slowest.
(b) By how many thousandths of a second did the winner beat the runner-up?
(c) Which girls ran under 14.25 seconds, and by how many thousandths does Esha miss that mark?
(d) Who should be the two team members and who, if anyone, may be the reserve? Justify with the differences.
questions.a: (a) Bhavna 14.082, Dolly 14.208, Esha 14.265, Aisha 14.28, Chitra 14.8. (b) 14.208 - 14.082 = 126 thousandths. (c) Bhavna and Dolly. Esha misses by 14.265 - 14.25 = 15 thousandths. (d) The team is Bhavna and Dolly. Esha is 15 thousandths (0.015 s) above the mark, within the 0.02 s allowed, so she may be reserve; Aisha is 30 thousandths (0.030 s) above, which is more than 0.02, so she cannot.
s: Part (a): orders Bhavna, Dolly, Esha, Aisha, Chitra
Part (c): Bhavna and Dolly under 14.25, Esha misses by 15 thousandths
Part (d): team Bhavna and Dolly; reserve Esha (0.015 within 0.02), not Aisha (0.030)

questions.q:
A school weather club in Chennai records rainfall each day in cm: Monday 12.305, Tuesday 12.35, Wednesday 12.053 and Thursday 12.5. The club will send a flood warning to the municipal office for any day on which the rainfall is more than 12.35 cm.
(a) Which day had the heaviest rain and which the lightest?
(b) Monday's and Tuesday's readings both lie in the same tenth-segment of the number line. Name its end points.
(c) By how many thousandths of a cm does Tuesday's reading exceed Monday's?
(d) On which days should the club send a warning? Justify your answer for Tuesday.
questions.a: (a) Heaviest: Thursday (12.5); lightest: Wednesday (12.053). (b) 12.3 and 12.4. (c) 12.350 - 12.305 = 45 thousandths. (d) Only Thursday: 12.5 > 12.35. Tuesday is exactly 12.35, which is not more than 12.35, so no warning for Tuesday under the stated rule.
s: Part (d): warns for Thursday only and justifies Tuesday as equal, not more

questions.q: A photocopy shop near a school in Bhopal charges 75 paise a page. (a) Write 75 paise in rupees. (b) A teacher gets 640 pages copied. What does she pay in rupees?
Pooja says 75 paise is ₹0.75. Arun says it is ₹7.5. Which of them is right? Prove it using fractions of a rupee.
questions.a: Pooja is right. 1 rupee = 100 paise, so 75 paise = 75/100 rupee = 70/100 + 5/100 = 7 tenths + 5 hundredths = ₹0.75. Arun's ₹7.5 is 75 tenths of a rupee, which is 750 paise, ten times too much.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says a sack of 2.5 kg weighs 250 g. Show that this cannot be right and give its weight in grams.
questions.a: 250 g is 250/1000 = 0.25 kg, which is a tenth of 2.5 kg. 2.5 kg = 2 kg + 0.5 kg = 2000 g + 500 g = 2500 g, so the sack cannot weigh 250 g.

questions.q: Make up a real-life situation in which a length of 58 cm has to be written in metres. Give the length in metres and show why that is correct.

questions.q: Radha's mother lists sugar 640 g, ghee 0.48 kg, rice 2.5 kg, salt 250 g and tea 95 g. (a) Write the three items given in grams in kilograms. (b) Arrange all five items from lightest to heaviest. (c) What is the combined weight of the sugar and the salt, in kilograms?

questions.q: A school stationery stall in Ranchi prices items as: pen 750 paise, notebook ₹18.5, ruler 1250 paise, eraser ₹4.05 and sharpener 305 paise. (a) Write every price in rupees as a decimal. (b) Which item is the costliest and which the cheapest? (c) How many paise is the notebook, and how many paise dearer is it than the ruler?
questions.a: (a) pen ₹7.5, notebook ₹18.5, ruler ₹12.5, eraser ₹4.05, sharpener ₹3.05. (b) Costliest: notebook (18.5); cheapest: sharpener (3.05). (c) 18.5 = 1850 paise; 1850 - 1250 = 600 paise dearer.

A museum in Kolkata is putting three small specimens in a display slot that is 2.0 cm wide. Its labels give: a hummingbird egg 1.3 cm long and 0.9 cm wide; a Philippine Goby about 0.9 cm long; and a Wolfi octopus, whose typical size ranges from 1 cm to 2.5 cm.
(a) Write the length and width of the egg in millimetres.
(b) Write the largest size of the octopus in metres.
(c) By how many millimetres is the egg's length less than the slot's width?
(d) Which specimens are certain to fit in the slot, and what should the museum do about the third?
questions.a: (a) 13 mm long and 9 mm wide. (b) 2.5 cm = 0.025 m. (c) The slot is 20 mm; 7 mm more than the egg's length. (d) The egg (13 mm) and the goby (9 mm) fit. The octopus may be up to 25 mm, which is more than 20 mm, so it may not fit; the museum should measure its actual specimen first or use a wider slot.
s: Part (d): egg and goby fit; octopus up to 25 mm may not, so measure it or widen the slot

questions.q:
Grandfather in Madurai remembers prices from the 1970s: a masala dosa cost 50 paise, a banana 25 paise and a kilogram of rice ₹2.45. One day he had exactly ₹3. He had to buy the rice, and he also wanted either the dosa or the banana. He needed to keep at least 20 paise for the bus fare home.
(a) Write the dosa and banana prices in rupees.
(b) Write the price of a kilogram of rice in paise.
(c) How much is left from ₹3 after buying the rice?
(d) Which treat can he afford, and why? Say how much remains in each case.
questions.a: (a) ₹0.50 and ₹0.25. (b) 245 paise. (c) 3.00 - 2.45 = ₹0.55 (55 paise). (d) Rice + dosa costs ₹2.95, leaving ₹0.05, which is less than the 20 paise needed for the bus. Rice + banana costs ₹2.70, leaving ₹0.30, which is enough. So he can afford the banana but not the dosa, even though the dosa is the bigger treat.
s: Part (d): dosa leaves 5 paise (too little), banana leaves 30 paise, so the banana

Arun adds 4.5 and 0.35 by writing 45 + 35 = 80 and answers 8.0. Find his error and give the correct sum.
questions.a: He lined up the last digits instead of the decimal points, so he added 5 tenths to 5 hundredths. Correct: 4.50 + 0.35 = 4.85.
s: Names the error: last digits aligned, not the decimal points

questions.q: Find 63.402 - 48.759. Show where you have to borrow.
questions.a: Thousandths: 2 < 9, so borrow from the hundredths; the 0 there borrows 1 tenth first (tenths 4 become 3), giving hundredths 9 and thousandths 12. Then 12 - 9 = 3, 9 - 5 = 4, and tenths 3 - 7 borrows 1 unit (13 - 7 = 6). Units 2 - 8 borrows 1 ten (12 - 8 = 4), then 5 - 4 = 1. Result: 14.643.
s: Shows the borrowing across thousandths, hundredths, tenths and units

questions.q: Add 19.99 and 6.01. Show the carries across the decimal point, and say why the answer is a whole number.
questions.a: Hundredths 9 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1 tenth); tenths 9 + 0 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1 unit); units 9 + 6 + 1 = 16 (write 6, carry 1 ten); tens 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. Sum = 26.00. The decimal parts 0.99 and 0.01 together make exactly 1.
s: Shows the carries from hundredths and tenths across the point, and on to the tens

questions.q: Neha works out 25 - 9.7 like this: '25 - 9 = 16, and the .7 just stays, so the answer is 16.7.' Find her error and give the correct answer.
questions.a: The 0.7 is being taken away as well, not kept. Write 25 as 24 and 10 tenths: 10 tenths - 7 tenths = 3 tenths, and 24 - 9 = 15, so 25 - 9.7 = 15.3. Her answer 16.7 is wrong; check: 15.3 + 9.7 = 25.
s: Names the error: the 0.7 must also be subtracted
Works out 15.3 by regrouping 25 as 24 and 10 tenths

questions.q: A student works out 12.65 - 4.8 and gets 8.25. Show by checking with addition that this cannot be right, then give the correct difference and the likely slip.
questions.a: If 8.25 were right, 8.25 + 4.8 would be 12.65, but 8.25 + 4.80 = 13.05. So 8.25 is wrong. The correct difference is 12.65 - 4.80 = 7.85. The slip: in the tenths column 6 - 8 cannot be done, so he took 8 - 6 = 2 and never borrowed from the units.
s: Says 13.05 is not 12.65 so 8.25 is impossible
Gives the correct difference 7.85 and names the borrowing slip

questions.q: Write a real-life word problem that is solved by finding 12.4 - 6.7, and solve it.
questions.a: Any suitable story, e.g. a tailor has 12.4 m of cloth and uses 6.7 m. Answer: 12.4 - 6.7 = 5.7 m, found by regrouping 12 units 4 tenths as 11 units 14 tenths.

questions.q: A cloth merchant in Surat buys rolls of 14.625 m, 8.75 m and 11.4 m and cuts 27.5 m for a uniform order. His assistant writes: '14.625 + 8.75 = 23.375; 23.375 + 11.4 = 34.775; 34.775 - 27.5 = 7.375.' (a) Check the total length. (b) Find the line in which the assistant went wrong and give the correct result. (c) Show how adding back catches the mistake. (d) By how much is the longest roll longer than the shortest?
questions.a: (a) 34.775 m, so the first two lines are right. (b) The last line is wrong: 34.775 - 27.500 = 7.275 m, not 7.375 (he is 1 tenth too high, a borrowing slip in the tenths). (c) 7.375 + 27.5 = 34.875, which is not 34.775, so 7.375 cannot be right; 7.275 + 27.5 = 34.775. (d) 14.625 - 8.75 = 5.875 m.
s: Part (b): finds the last line wrong and gives 7.275 m
Part (c): adds back to get 34.875 and compares with 34.775

The Class 7 teachers in a school in Coimbatore collect picnic money: Section A pays ₹3,480.75 and Section B pays ₹2,915.50. The bus costs ₹4,250.25. The caterer quotes ₹2,198.40 for the standard lunch (with sweets) or ₹2,139.85 for a smaller menu (no sweets). The principal says she will add ₹60.00 if asked in writing today.

questions.a: (a) 3,480.75 + 2,915.50 = ₹6,396.25. (b) 6,396.25 - 4,250.25 = ₹2,146.00. (c) 2,198.40 - 2,146.00 = ₹52.40. Either can be defended: the standard lunch gives sweets for ₹52.40 of outside money; the smaller menu keeps the class independent of outside money.
s: Part (d): compares ₹7.60 left with the principal's help against ₹6.15 left without it, and justifies a choice

questions.q: (a) Between which whole numbers must 31.6 + 12.45 lie? (b) A student guesses 44.5. Can the range rule it out? Find the exact sum.
questions.a: (a) 31 + 12 = 43, so the sum lies between 43 and 45. (b) No: 44.5 is inside 43 to 45, so the range cannot reject it. The exact sum 31.60 + 12.45 = 44.05 shows the guess is wrong.
s: Part (b): says the range cannot rule it out and finds 44.05

questions.q: Explain why the sum of two decimals is always less than 2 more than the sum of their whole-number parts.
questions.a: Each decimal is its whole part plus a fractional part, and a fractional part is less than 1. Two such parts together are less than 1 + 1 = 2, so the sum is less than the whole parts' sum plus 2.
s: States each decimal = whole part + a fractional part below 1
Adds the two fractional parts to get less than 2

questions.q: Two decimals have whole parts 40 and 17. Write the range for their difference, and give a pair of decimals whose difference is near the bottom of that range.

questions.q: Rishi says: '9.1 - 4.9 lies between 4 and 6.' Is he right? Use the whole-number parts, and say why the range runs from 4 and not from 5.
questions.a: Yes. The whole parts give 9 - 4 = 5, and the difference of two decimals lies within 1 of that, so between 4 and 6. Exact: 9.1 - 4.9 = 4.2, which is inside the range. It is below 5 because 9.1 has only 0.1 above 9 while 4.9 has 0.9 above 4, so the fractional parts reduce the difference; the range must allow for that.
s: Gives the verdict that Rishi is right
Checks the exact value 4.2 and explains why it falls below 5

questions.q: Someone says 14.9 + 9.9 = 26. Show that this cannot be correct without adding the decimals, and then find the true sum.
questions.a: Whole parts 14 and 9 give 23, so the sum lies between 23 and 25. 26 is outside that range, so it cannot be right. True sum: 14.9 + 9.9 = 24.8.
s: Finds the whole parts' sum 23 and the range 23 to 25
Says 26 is outside the range so it is impossible

questions.q: Write two decimals whose whole parts are 8 and 9 and whose sum is above 18.5. Show with the estimation rule that the sum cannot reach 19, and find the actual sum.
questions.a: For example 8.95 + 9.95 = 18.90. The whole parts add to 17, so the sum lies between 17 and 19, and 18.9 is above 18.5 but below 19. Any valid pair works if the sum is above 18.5.
s: Gives two valid decimals with whole parts 8 and 9
States the range 17 to 19 from the whole parts
Shows the actual sum is above 18.5 and below 19

questions.q: Estimate first and then calculate. (a) Give the range for 46.8 + 29.35. (b) Find its exact value. (c) Give the range for 46.8 - 29.35. (d) Find its exact value. (e) Do both exact values lie in their ranges?
s: Part (e): checks both values against their ranges

questions.q: At a school fair in Guwahati the morning collection was ₹4,372.60 and the afternoon collection ₹2,985.75. The treasurer reports the total as ₹7,458.35. (a) Use the whole-number parts to give a range for the total. (b) Does the reported total lie in the range? (c) Find the exact total. (d) By how much is the treasurer's figure out, and what kind of slip does that suggest?
questions.a: (a) 4372 + 2985 = 7357, so the total is between 7357 and 7359. (b) No: 7,458.35 is above 7359. (c) 4,372.60 + 2,985.75 = ₹7,358.35. (d) 7,458.35 - 7,358.35 = ₹100.00; the figure is exactly ₹100 too high, which suggests a wrong digit in the hundreds place.
s: Part (b): says the reported total is outside the range
Part (d): says a hundreds-place digit slip is suggested

questions.q:
In a charity walk, Meera walked 12.85 km on Saturday and 9.6 km on Sunday. The walk gives a badge to anyone who covers at least 22.5 km over the two days.
(a) Using only the whole-number parts, between which two numbers does her total lie?
(b) Can this range alone tell the coach whether Meera earned the badge? Explain.
(c) Find her exact total distance.
(d) Does she earn the badge, and by how much does her total differ from the target?
questions.a: (a) 12 + 9 = 21, so the total is between 21 and 23. (b) No: the target 22.5 lies inside the range 21 to 23, so the total could be on either side of it. (c) 12.85 + 9.60 = 22.45 km. (d) No. 22.5 - 22.45 = 0.05 km; she is 0.05 km (50 metres) short.
s: Part (b): says the target 22.5 lies inside the range so it cannot decide
Part (d): no badge, short by 0.05 km

questions.q:
A family travelling by train from Pune to Chennai packs two bags weighing 18.75 kg and 21.6 kg. The free baggage allowance is 40 kg. Excess baggage is charged ₹300 whatever the extra weight. To avoid the charge they could leave behind either a 0.3 kg storybook (free to leave) or a 0.5 kg jar of home-made pickle that would cost ₹450 to buy again at the destination.
(a) Using whole-number parts, give the range for the total weight and say whether it decides if they are within 40 kg.
(b) Find the exact total weight.
(c) Which option should the family choose: pay ₹300, leave the book, or leave the pickle? Justify with the new total weight for each option.
questions.a: (a) 18 + 21 = 39, so the total is between 39 and 41. The range cannot decide because 40 lies inside it. (b) 18.75 + 21.60 = 40.35 kg, which is 0.35 kg over. (c) Leaving the book gives 40.05 kg, still over 40, so it does not avoid the charge. Leaving the pickle gives 39.85 kg, which is within 40 but costs ₹450 to replace. Paying ₹300 is cheaper than losing the pickle, so the family should pay the ₹300 (unless they value the pickle less than ₹300).
s: Part (a): range 39 to 41 and says it cannot decide since 40 lies inside
Part (c): new totals 40.05 and 39.85, then compares ₹300 with ₹450 and decides

questions.a: 3 overs and 4 balls are left

questions.q: Which of these decimal-looking quantities is NOT an ordinary base-ten decimal?
questions.a: 5.4 overs

questions.a: 30 minutes

questions.a: 6 minutes

questions.q: A school-bus app messages: 'The bus will reach the stop 8.5 hours after midnight.' When will the bus arrive?
At a school cricket match the scoreboard reads 'Overs bowled: 12.4'. How many balls have been bowled?

Consider the statements about decimal-looking numbers.
Statement 1: 'Overs left: 5.5' means 5 and 5/10 overs.
Statement 2: 3.4 overs bowled means 3 overs and 4 balls.
Statement 3: In '4.5 hours after noon' the 0.5 stands for 30 minutes.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In 'Overs left: 5.5' the digit 5 after the point stands for 5 balls.
Reason (R): One over has 6 balls, so the digit after the point in an overs score can be as large as 6.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: In a 20-over match the scoreboard shows 'Overs left: 6.2'. (a) How many balls are left? (b) How many overs have been bowled? Write it as the scoreboard would.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 6 + 2 = 38 balls. (b) 20 overs = 120 balls, so 82 balls have been bowled, which is 13.4 overs on the scoreboard.

questions.q: (a) Write 2.4 hours in hours and minutes. (b) Is that the same as 2 hours 40 minutes? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 0.4 hour = 4 tenths of an hour = 4 x 6 = 24 minutes, so 2 h 24 min (2 h 24 min). (b) No. 40 minutes would be 4/6 of an hour, but 0.4 hour is 4/10 of an hour; an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
s: Part (a): 4 x 6 = 24 minutes, so 2 h 24 min
Part (b): says it is not 2 h 40 min, as an hour is 60 minutes and not 10 tenths of 10 minutes

questions.q: Why should 'Overs left: 5.5' not be read like the decimal 5.5, meaning 5 and 5 tenths? What does it mean?
questions.a: In an overs score the digit after the point counts balls out of 6, not tenths. 5.5 overs is 5 overs and 5 balls, i.e. 5 and 5/6 overs, not 5 and 5/10.
s: States the digit after the point counts balls and an over has 6 balls
Gives the meaning 5 overs and 5 balls (5 5/6 overs)

questions.q: Ritu measures a window frame as 3 ft 4 in but tells the carpenter 'make it 3.4 ft'. (a) What width in inches does 0.4 ft stand for? (b) Is the window he builds wider or narrower than the frame, and by how many inches? (1 ft = 12 in.)
questions.a: (a) 0.4 ft = 4 tenths of 12 in = 4.8 in. (b) The window is 3 ft 4.8 in, wider than the frame by 4.8 - 4 = 0.8 in, so it will not fit.

questions.q: After 5.5 overs one more ball is bowled. What does the scoreboard show, and why is it not 5.6?
questions.a: It shows 6.0. 5.5 overs is 5 overs and 5 balls; one more ball makes 6 balls, which is a full over, so the scoreboard goes to 6 overs and 0 balls.
s: Explains 6 balls make one over so the digit after the point cannot be 6

questions.q: Zoya says: '2.5 hours means 2 hours 50 minutes, because 0.5 is 50 hundredths.' Is she right? Explain what 2.5 hours really is.
questions.a: No. An hour has 60 minutes and is split into 10 parts of 6 minutes each. 0.5 hour is 5 such parts, 5 x 6 = 30 minutes, so 2.5 hours is 2 hours 30 minutes. Hundredths do not apply because the hour is not divided by 100 minutes.
s: Gives the verdict that Zoya is wrong
Shows each tenth of an hour is 6 minutes
Gets 5 x 6 = 30 minutes, so 2 hours 30 minutes

questions.q: Show that a scoreboard cannot correctly read 'Overs bowled: 7.8'. What would it show after 7 overs and 8 balls?
questions.a: An over has 6 balls, so the digit after the point can only be 0 to 5. 8 balls would complete one over (6 balls) and leave 2, so the bowling is 8 overs and 2 balls. The board would show 8.2.
s: States an over has 6 balls so the digit after the point is at most 5
Breaks 8 balls into one over and 2 balls

questions.q: Make up a short real-life message or notice that uses a decimal-looking time or an overs score. Say how a careless reader could misread it and what it really means.
questions.a: Any valid example, e.g. 'The match resumes after 1.5 hours': a careless reader may think 1 h 50 min or 1 h 5 min, but 0.5 hour is 30 minutes so it means 1 h 30 min. Or '10.3 overs' read as 10 and 3/10 instead of 10 overs and 3 balls.
s: A realistic message using a time or an overs score
Gives the correct meaning with the 60-minute or 6-ball reasoning

questions.q: In a 20-over school match in Visakhapatnam the scoreboard reads 'Overs bowled: 14.3'. (a) How many balls have been bowled? (b) How many balls are left in the innings? (c) Write the overs left as the scoreboard shows them. (d) After 2 more overs and 4 more balls, what will the scoreboard read for overs bowled?
questions.a: (a) 14 x 6 + 3 = 87 balls. (b) 120 - 87 = 33 balls. (c) 33 = 5 x 6 + 3, so 5.3 overs left. (d) 2.4 overs is 16 balls; 87 + 16 = 103 balls = 17.1. The board reads 17.1.
s: Part (d): adds 16 balls to get 103 balls

questions.q: A bus leaves Hyderabad at 6:00 a.m. and the booking message says the journey takes 5.4 hours. (a) Write 5.4 hours in hours and minutes. (b) At what time does the bus arrive? (c) A friend reads 5.4 hours as 5 hours 40 minutes. By how many minutes does the arrival time he expects differ from the true arrival time, and is it earlier or later? (d) Explain in one line why 0.4 hour is not 40 minutes.
questions.a: (a) 0.4 x 60 = 24, so 5 h 24 min. (b) 6:00 + 5 h 24 min = 11:24 a.m. (c) He expects 11:40 a.m., which is 16 minutes later than the true arrival at 11:24, so he would reach the station 16 minutes after the bus is already there. (d) An hour has 60 minutes; one-tenth of it is 6 minutes, so 4 tenths is 24 minutes.
s: Part (c): friend expects 11:40 a.m., 16 minutes later than the true time
Part (d): one tenth of an hour is 6 minutes

questions.q:
In a 20-over school cricket final in Jaipur, the scoreboard shows 'Overs bowled: 16.4'. The spinner has bowled 3.4 overs and the fast bowler Kabir has bowled 2.2 overs; a bowler may bowl at most 4 overs (24 balls) in the match. Kabir wants to bowl the final over of the innings.
(a) How many balls have been bowled so far, and how many remain?
(b) How many balls may the spinner still bowl?
(c) How many balls may Kabir still bowl? Does that allow him to bowl the final over of 6 balls?
(d) If the spinner and Kabir bowl all the balls they are allowed, how many of the remaining balls must other bowlers bowl? Write this as the scoreboard would write overs.
questions.a: (a) 16 x 6 + 4 = 100 balls bowled; 120 - 100 = 20 balls remain. (b) 3.4 overs = 22 balls, so 24 - 22 = 2 balls. (c) 2.2 overs = 14 balls, so Kabir has 24 - 14 = 10 balls left; 10 is more than 6, so he can bowl the final over. (d) 20 - 2 - 10 = 8 balls, which is written 1.2 overs.
s: Part (b): the spinner has 2 balls left
Part (c): Kabir has 10 balls left, so the final over of 6 is allowed

questions.q:
Karan must catch a train at 11:55 a.m. from a station in Bengaluru. A bus leaves the bus stand at 9:20 a.m. and the booking message says the journey takes 2.4 hours. After the bus reaches the station area, he needs 10 minutes to walk to the train platform.
(a) Write 2.4 hours in hours and minutes.
(b) At what time does the bus reach the station area?
(c) At what time would he reach the platform?
(d) Should Karan take this bus? Explain, and say how Karan's plan changes if the message had meant 2 hours 40 minutes instead.
questions.a: (a) 0.4 x 60 = 24, so 2 h 24 min. (b) 9:20 + 2 h 24 min = 11:44 a.m. (c) 11:44 + 10 min = 11:54 a.m. (d) He reaches the platform at 11:54, a minute before 11:55, so the plan works but is very tight. If the message meant 2 h 40 min the bus would arrive at 12:00 and he would miss the train, so he should be sure that 2.4 hours means 2 h 24 min; given that, the bus works but with only 1 minute to spare.
s: Part (d): says the plan works with 1 minute to spare and compares with the 2 h 40 min reading (12:00)

questions.q: Which of these decimals is closest to 3?
A decimal is 'closest' to a target number when
questions.a: its difference from the target is the smallest
o: its difference from the target is the smallest
it is the smallest number larger than the target
it is smaller than the target

questions.q: What is the constant change in the sequence 3.2, 3.7, 4.2, 4.7, ...?
Tanvi saves ₹12.50 in the first week, ₹13.75 in the second and ₹15.00 in the third, and keeps the same pattern. How much does she save in the fourth week?
Fatima needs a ribbon as close to 1 m as possible. The pieces in the shop measure 0.8 m, 0.69 m, 1.08 m and 0.95 m. Which should she buy?
What is the next term of the sequence 7.5, 8.3, 9.1, ...?

Consider the statements.
Statement 1: To find the change in a decimal sequence we subtract each term from the next term.
Statement 2: A decimal that is below the target can never be the closest one to it.
Statement 3: In 13.5, 16, 18.5 the change is 2.5.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 1.01 is closer to 1 than 0.9 is.
Reason (R): The sequence 3, 2.96, 2.92, 2.88 goes down by 0.04 each time.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Which sequence does NOT have a constant change between neighbouring terms?
(a) Which of 6.58, 6.85 and 6.099 is closest to 7? (b) By how many hundredths does it differ from 7?
questions.a: (a) The differences from 7 are 0.42, 0.15 and 0.901, so 6.85 is closest. (b) 7 - 6.85 = 0.15, which is 15 hundredths.
s: Part (a): finds the three differences and picks 6.85

questions.q: Look at the sequence 20.8, 20.35, 19.9, ... (a) What is the change after each term? (b) Write the next two terms.
questions.a: (a) Each term is 0.45 less than the one before (20.8 - 20.35 = 0.45). (b) 19.9 - 0.45 = 19.45; then 19.0.

questions.q: Using the digits 1, 5, 7 and 9 exactly once each and one decimal point, make the decimal closest to 20. Give its difference from 20.
questions.a: 19.75 is the closest: 20 - 19.75 = 0.25. Others like 19.57 (0.43) and 17.95 (2.05) are further away.

questions.q: Which of 2.97 and 3.04 is closer to 3? Give each difference in hundredths.
questions.a: 2.97 is 3 hundredths below 3 (3.00 - 2.97 = 0.03) and 3.04 is 4 hundredths above 3. So 2.97 is closer.

questions.q: Write the first four terms of a sequence that starts at 9.5 and goes down by 1.25 each time.
Anika says: 'Among 3.2, 3.099 and 2.95, the number closest to 3 is 2.95, even though it is smaller than 3.' Is she right? Support your answer with the differences.
questions.a: Yes. The differences from 3 are 0.2 (3.2), 0.099 (3.099) and 0.05 (2.95). 0.05 = 50 thousandths is the smallest, so 2.95 is closest. Being below the target does not matter; only the size of the difference does.
s: Gives the verdict that Anika is right
Concludes the smallest difference decides, whether above or below 3

questions.q: Show that 7.5, 8.3 and 9.2 cannot be consecutive terms of a sequence with a constant change.
questions.a: The change from 7.5 to 8.3 is 0.8 but from 8.3 to 9.2 it is 0.9. A constant change would give the same difference both times, and 0.8 is not 0.9.
s: Concludes the changes differ so no constant change is possible

questions.q: Write a sequence of five decimals that starts at 2.4 and has a constant change of 0.35. Then make up a real-life situation in which such a sequence could occur.
questions.a: 2.40, 2.75, 3.10, 3.45, 3.80. Situation example: a plant grows 0.35 cm every day from a height of 2.4 cm.
s: Writes the five terms starting 2.4 with the correct change
A realistic situation with a constant change of 0.35

questions.q: Look at the sequence 1.2, 2.1, 2.09, 2.99, 2.98, 3.88, ... (a) Describe the two changes that alternate. (b) Write the next four terms. (c) Find the 10th term. (d) What is the total change over every two steps, and how does it help you check the 9th term?
questions.a: (a) Alternately add 0.9 and subtract 0.01. (b) 3.87, 4.77, 4.76, 5.66. (c) The 10th term is 5.66. (d) Every two steps change the value by 0.9 - 0.01 = 0.89. The 9th term is 1.2 + 4 x 0.89 = 4.76, which matches.
s: Part (d): net 0.89 per two steps and checks the 9th term 4.76

questions.q: Use the digits 2, 7, 0, 5 and 9 exactly once each, with one decimal point and with no zero at the start of a whole part. (a) Make the decimal closest to 60. (b) Make the smallest decimal between 100 and 1000. (c) How far is your answer in (a) from 60?
questions.a: (a) 59.720, using 5, 9 in the whole part and 7, 2, 0 after the point. (b) 205.79: the smallest possible hundreds digit is 2, then 0, then 5, with 7 and 9 after the point. (c) 60 - 59.72 = 0.28, i.e. 28 hundredths.
s: Part (b): 205.79 with the reason for the smallest digits in the highest places

questions.q:
A packing unit in Rajkot fills sugar bags labelled 1 kg. An inspector weighs five bags: 0.985 kg, 1.01 kg, 0.9 kg, 1.1 kg and 1.004 kg. A bag passes if its weight is within 0.01 kg of 1 kg (exactly 0.01 kg away still passes). The manager says the machine always under-fills.
(a) Which bag is closest to 1 kg, and by how many thousandths?
(b) Which bags pass the rule?
(c) Do the five readings support the manager's claim? Justify, and say what the readings suggest about the machine.
questions.a: (a) 1.004 kg, 4 thousandths away (1.01 is 10 thousandths away). (b) 1.004 and 1.01 pass; 0.985 is 15 thousandths away, which is too far. (c) No. Three bags are above 1 kg (1.01, 1.1, 1.004) and two are below (0.985, 0.9), so the machine does not always under-fill. The errors of 0.1 kg in both directions (0.9 and 1.1) suggest it is inconsistent and needs a check, not just one adjustment.
s: Part (c): shows bags both above and below 1 kg so the claim fails, and suggests an inconsistent machine

questions.q:
Tanvi and her sister Isha each save part of their pocket money in rupees every month. Tanvi saves ₹25.50 in January, ₹28.25 in February and ₹31.00 in March. Isha saves ₹40.00 in January, ₹38.25 in February and ₹36.50 in March. Both keep the same constant change each month.
(a) What is Tanvi's monthly change?
(b) How much does Tanvi save in May?
(c) How much does Isha save in May?
(d) Tanvi says she is the better saver because her savings keep rising while Isha's keep falling. Over the five months January to May, who has saved more in total? Support your answer with the totals.
questions.a: (a) 28.25 - 25.50 = ₹2.75 more each month. (b) April ₹33.75, May ₹36.50. (c) Isha's change is -1.75 each month: April ₹34.75, May ₹33.00. (d) Tanvi's five-month total is ₹155.00; Isha's is ₹182.50. Isha has saved ₹27.50 more in total, although Tanvi's monthly saving has overtaken hers by May.
s: Part (d): totals 155.00 and 182.50, so Isha saved ₹27.50 more
